title: Improvise a funnel
mechanism_check: A funnel is a cone with a spout: wide mouth to catch, narrow exit to direct.
Match the spout to the receiving opening and the cone to the pour volume.
improvised_tools: A plastic bottle cut in half (top half = funnel); a sheet of paper or card rolled into a cone.
Tape to hold the cone shape; scissors or a knife to cut.
steps: Cut the bottle about two-thirds up; the top half with the neck is your funnel.
For paper: roll a cone, tape the seam, snip the tip to size.
Seat the spout in the receiving opening before pouring.
Pour slowly — improvised funnels clog and overflow faster than real ones.
stop_conditions: Hot liquids in a thin plastic bottle funnel: it softens and collapses — use paper/metal instead.
Chemicals or fuel: use compatible materials only; paper and fuel are a bad pair.

title: Cut a straight line with no saw guide
mechanism_check: Straight cuts come from the guide, not the hand — the saw follows the fence.
Any straight, clampable edge works as a fence: factory edge of plywood, a level, a 2x4.
improvised_tools: The factory edge of a sheet good, a spirit level, or a straight 2x4 as the fence.
Two clamps (or screws through waste areas) to fix the fence.
A sharp knife to score the line first — the score steers the saw.
steps: Mark the cut line and the waste side with an X.
Clamp the fence parallel to the line, offset by the saw's blade-to-base distance.
Score the line with a knife to prevent tear-out.
Cut with the saw base riding the fence; steady pace, no forcing.
stop_conditions: Fence shifting mid-cut: stop and re-clamp — a moved fence ruins the cut.
No way to clamp safely: stop — a hand-held 'fence' is how cuts go crooked and fingers get close.

title: Measure without a tape measure
mechanism_check: Measurement is comparison to a known unit — your body carries several.
Body units vary person to person: calibrate yours once against a real ruler.
improvised_tools: Your own calibrated spans: hand span, forearm (cubit), foot length, arm span.
Paper currency and cards have exact standard dimensions — a ruler in your wallet.
A piece of string marked with knots at your calibrated units.
steps: Calibrate: measure your hand span, foot, and arm span against a real ruler once.
Write the numbers down (phone note) so you don't rely on memory.
Measure with the body unit, then sanity-check with a second method.
For critical cuts, borrow or buy a real tape — body units are for layout, not joinery.
stop_conditions: Tolerance tighter than ~1/4 inch: stop estimating and get a real measuring tool.
Anyone else building from your numbers: convert to real units first — your cubit isn't theirs.

title: Improvise a clamp
mechanism_check: A clamp is two jaws + a screw: pressure from a small contact area.
Match the clamp to the job: light positioning vs glue-up pressure are different beasts.
improvised_tools: Rope tourniquet: loop around the work, twist a stick in the loop to tighten.
Wedge clamp: two wedges driven against each other between the work and a fixed stop.
Heavy objects (paint cans, toolboxes) as dead-weight clamps for flat glue-ups.
steps: Position the work exactly — improvised clamps shift things as they tighten.
Apply the tourniquet/wedges/weight and check alignment before full pressure.
Protect the work with scrap pads under every contact point.
Leave glue-ups undisturbed for the full cure time.
stop_conditions: Joint shifting under improvised pressure: stop and re-fixture — a glued joint cures where it sits.
Need for high, even pressure (bent laminations): stop — that's real-clamp territory.

title: Hone a dull knife with no stone
mechanism_check: A dull knife usually has a rolled edge, not a missing edge — honing straightens the roll.
The unglazed ring on the bottom of a ceramic mug is a fine abrasive, like a honing steel.
improvised_tools: The unglazed foot ring of a ceramic mug or plate.
A leather belt as a strop for the final polish.
A steady surface — the mug must not move.
steps: Flip the mug upside down on a damp towel so it can't slide.
Hold the knife at ~20 degrees to the ceramic ring.
Draw the blade across the ring heel-to-tip, alternating sides, light pressure.
Strop on the belt a few passes per side; test on paper.
stop_conditions: Chips or a broken tip: honing won't fix it — that's grinding/reshaping work.
Knife flexing or your grip slipping: stop — a sharp knife and a bad grip is how cuts happen.

title: Open a stuck jar lid
mechanism_check: Vacuum seal + sticky residue lock the lid; breaking the vacuum or the sticky bond frees it.
Grip is usually the real problem — the lid is fine, your hand slips.
improvised_tools: A rubber glove, rubber band, or damp towel for grip.
A spoon handle under the lid edge to break the vacuum (gentle pry).
Hot water on the metal lid to expand it.
steps: Improve grip first: rubber glove or rubber band around the lid.
Tap the lid edge firmly on the counter to break the seal.
Run hot water over the lid for 30 seconds to expand the metal.
Pry gently under the edge with a spoon to hiss the vacuum out, then twist.
stop_conditions: Lid bending or glass chipping under prying: stop — glass shards beat a stuck jar.
Bulging lid or foul smell on opening: do not taste — spoilage signs mean discard.

title: Design the tool from the job backwards (the CREATE method)
mechanism_check: Every tool is an answer to a force-and-geometry question: what must move, how far, with what precision?
Design from the workpiece backwards: contact point -> force path -> handle -> your body.
The create track asks 'what should exist?' where improvise asks 'what can I use?'
improvised_tools: Paper and pencil: sketch the force path before building anything.
Scrap stock for a mockup — prove the geometry with a crude version first.
steps: Write the job as one sentence: 'I need to hold X still while Y turns.'
Name the pattern: grip, torque, wedge, lever, guide, measure.
Sketch the contact point first, then work backwards to your hands.
Build the crudest version that tests the geometry; refine only what the test proves wrong.
stop_conditions: The design needs precision you can't verify: stop — an unmeasurable tool is a guess.
Safety-critical loads (lifting, life safety): stop designing and buy the engineered tool.

title: Combine scrap parts into a shop organizer
mechanism_check: An organizer is just compartments sized to contents + a structure that holds them.
Sort first by use: the things you grab together live together.
Scrap is free but irregular — design around the pieces you actually have.
improvised_tools: Offcuts, old drawers, cans, jars, cardboard boxes as compartments.
Screws and glue to join; a back board to mount it all on.
steps: Empty the bench and sort everything by use-family.
Lay out compartments on the floor sized to the actual items.
Build the carcass from the biggest scraps; fit compartments into it.
Mount at working height; label everything — the system only works if things go home.
stop_conditions: Organizer growing bigger than the bench: stop — you're building furniture, not organizing.
Heavy items up high in a flimsy carcass: stop — anchor it or redesign before it tips.

title: Design a wall-mounted storage shelf from the load down
mechanism_check: A shelf is a load path: board to brackets to wall anchors to studs.
Failure happens at the weakest link — usually the wall attachment, not the board.
Design the attachment first and the shelf second.
improvised_tools: A cardboard mockup of the shelf to test clearances before drilling.
A bathroom scale plus books to proof-load one bracket before mounting.
steps: List what goes on the shelf and weigh the heaviest zone.
Space brackets by load, not by looks — heavy spans get more brackets.
Find studs, or size anchors to the actual wall material.
Mount brackets dead level, then the board; load gradually and watch for creep.
stop_conditions: Masonry or tile you cannot anchor into properly: stop — a shelf that pulls out is a falling hazard.
Load keeps growing past the design: stop — redesign for the real load, don't hope.

title: Turn a ladder and planks into a work platform
mechanism_check: Two ladders plus planks is a scaffold: planks carry you, ladders carry the planks.
Every plank needs solid bearing on both ladders with overlap to spare.
Lateral wobble is what fails, not vertical load.
improvised_tools: Two matching stepladders; planks or a door slab for the deck.
Rope or straps to tie the ladders against spreading.
steps: Set both ladders on firm, level ground, fully opened and locked.
Tie the spreaders so neither ladder can fold.
Lay planks across with at least a foot of bearing on each ladder.
Test with body weight before bringing tools up; keep the work zone between the ladders, never at the plank tips.
stop_conditions: Ground soft or sloped: stop — a ladder that sinks on one side tips the whole platform.
Only one ladder, or planks too short for real bearing: stop — do not build it.
